title: Configuring Windows Server Hybrid Advanced Services (AZ-801)

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.
Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.
Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

questions.q: Your security team wants domain controllers to refuse to cache the credentials of administrative accounts if they are ever logged on to lower-trust member servers, so that a compromised member server cannot replay or extract those credentials. Which Active Directory feature should you implement to protect privileged accounts in this way?
choices: Add the privileged accounts to the Protected Users global security group
Enable Credential Guard with virtualization-based security on every member server
Configure a fine-grained password policy that increases the password length for administrators
Enable Kerberos armoring (Flexible Authentication Secure Tunneling) on every member server
questions.explanation: Membership in the Protected Users group hardens privileged accounts at the directory level: NTLM authentication, DES and RC4 encryption in Kerberos, unconstrained delegation, and the caching of cached credentials are all blocked, and Kerberos ticket lifetimes are capped at 4 hours. Credential Guard protects LSA secrets on the local machine but does not change what AD itself returns. Fine-grained password policies only affect password complexity. Kerberos armoring (FAST) protects the Kerberos exchange but not the broader credential surface that Protected Users covers.

questions.q: A regulated workload running on Windows Server 2022 must be able to run only an explicit allow-list of binaries — including PowerShell scripts and MSI installers — even if an administrator with local privileges attempts to launch an unsigned tool. The policy must be enforced by code integrity at the kernel and user-mode layers, not by a user-space service that an administrator can stop. Which control should you deploy?
choices: AppLocker rules enforced through Group Policy
User Account Control (UAC) at the highest prompt level
questions.explanation: Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) is enforced by the kernel through the code-integrity subsystem and cannot be bypassed by stopping a service — that is its main advantage over AppLocker, which runs as the AppIDSvc user-mode service and can be disabled by a local administrator. SRP is deprecated. UAC controls elevation prompts, not which binaries are allowed to execute.

questions.q: You manage roughly 200 on-premises and multi-cloud servers that are connected to Azure with Azure Arc. The compliance team wants Microsoft Defender for Cloud to perform agentless and agent-based threat detection, file integrity monitoring, and vulnerability assessment against those Arc-enabled servers. Which Defender for Cloud plan must be enabled to deliver this coverage on Arc-enabled servers?
choices: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 only
questions.explanation: Defender for Servers Plan 2 is the Defender for Cloud plan that targets servers — including Azure Arc-enabled machines outside Azure — and delivers Defender for Endpoint integration, file integrity monitoring, just-in-time VM access, adaptive application controls, and the integrated vulnerability assessment (formerly Qualys, now MDVM). Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 is the EDR product alone, without the Defender for Cloud server-protection extras. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB; Defender for Identity protects AD DS by analysing domain controller traffic, not general server posture.

questions.q: You are tightening administrative access to a tier-0 Windows Server 2022 jump host. Operators currently have local Administrators group membership, but auditors require that they only get the specific cmdlets they need to do their job, on demand, with their actions logged and their session run under a temporary virtual account that has no persistent privileges. Which Windows Server feature should you implement?
choices: Restricted Groups defined in a Group Policy Object
Just Enough Administration (JEA) using PowerShell session configurations and role capability files
Authentication Policies and Authentication Policy Silos
User Rights Assignment policies set to deny network logon
questions.explanation: Just Enough Administration (JEA) was designed for exactly this scenario. You define role capability files that whitelist the cmdlets, functions, and providers an operator may run, register a constrained PowerShell session configuration, and connections to that endpoint execute under a per-session virtual account that exists only for the lifetime of the session. Every command is transcribed and logged. Restricted Groups manage who is in a local group but do not constrain what they can run. Authentication Policy Silos restrict where credentials can be used, not which cmdlets are exposed. User Rights Assignment changes broad logon rights, not application-level command scope.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
